¶ '''trencher-critic''' (tren′chėr-krit″ik), ''n.'' A person curious in cookery and table-service; a gourmet. '''trencher-fly†''' (tren′chėr-flī), ''n.'' One who haunts the tables of others; a parasite. {{smaller block|Or otherwise delighted
In keeping Dogs and Horses, or by hearing
His ''trencher-Flies'' about his table jearing. {{right|''Heywood'', Dialogues (Works, ed. Pearson, 1874, VI. 171).}}}} '''trencher-friend''' (tren′chėr-frend), ''n.'' One who flatters another for the sake of a place at his table; a sponger. {{smaller block|You fools of fortune, ''trencher-friends'', time's flies! {{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., iii. 6. 106.}}}} '''trencher-knight''' (tren′chėr-nīt), ''n.'' A serving-man attending at table; a waiter. {{smaller block|Some ''trencher-knight'', some Dick,
That smiles his cheek in years, and knows the trick
To make my lady laugh. {{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. 2. 464.}}}} '''trencher-law''' (tren′chėr-lâ), ''n.'' The regulation of diet; dietetics. {{smaller block|When spleenish morsels cram the gaping maw,
Withouten diet's care, or ''trencher-law.'' {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Satires, IV. iv. 21.}}}} '''trencher-loaf†''' (tren′chėr-lōf), ''n.'' [< ME. ''trenchoure lofe''; < ''trencher''2 + ''loaf''1.] Same as ''trencher-bread.'' {{smaller block|Ye muste haue thre pantry knyues, one knyfe to square ''trenchoure loues'', an other to be a chyppere, the thyrde shall be sharpe to make smothe trenchoures. {{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 265.}}}}

'''trennel''' (tren′l), ''n.'' A corrupt form of ''treenail.''

'''trent<sup>1</sup>''' (trent), ''v. t.'' Same as ''trend''<sup>2</sup>.

'''trent<sup>2</sup>†''' (trent), ''n.'' [< ME. ''trent, trente,'' < OF. (and F.) ''trente,'' thirty, < L. ''triginta,'' thirty: see ''thirty.''] The number thirty; a trental.

{{smaller block|On the morwe to seie a ''trent'' of masses atte same ffreres.
{{right|''English Gilds'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 8.}}}}

'''trental''' (tren′tal), ''n.'' [< ME. ''trental, trentel,'' < OF. ''trentel, trental'' (ML. reflex ''trentale''), a trental, set of thirty masses (ML. *''trigintalia,'' pl.), < ''trente,'' thirty, < L. ''triginta,'' thirty: see ''trent''<sup>2</sup>.] A collection or series of anything numbering thirty; specifically, a service of thirty masses for a deceased person in the Roman Catholic Church on as many successive days, or formerly sometimes in one day. Also rarely ''trigintal.''

{{smaller block|"''Trentals,''" seyde he, "deliveren fro penaunce
Hir freendes soules, as wel olde as yonge."
{{right|''Chaucer,'' Summoner's Tale, l. 16.}}
A ''trental'' (thirty) of masses used to be offered up for almost every one on the burial day.
{{right|''Rock,'' Church of our Fathers, ii. 504, note.}}}}

'''Trenton limestone.''' See ''limestone.''

The animal is repulsive, somewhat resembling a stout worm in shape, but having rows of processes on its body, and others radiated about the mouth. It varies in length from 6 to 24 inches. Much skill and care are required in the operation of curing, which is performed by gutting and boiling these sea-slugs, and spreading them out on a perforated platform over a wood-fire (or sometimes in the sun) to dry. Sun-dried trepangs are in special request in China for making soups. The fishery is carried on in numerous localities in the Indian Ocean, in the Eastern Archipelago, and on the shores of Australia.}} [[File:century v08 p0263 c3f1.png|center|311px]] {{c|Trepang (''Holothuria edulis'').}} ¶ '''trepanize''' (trep′an-īz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''trepanized'', ppr.
